results.title: AI Can Make Investment Experiences Smarter, More Contextual and More Connected: ViewTrade
results.description: Artificial Intelligence is moving beyond being a technology experiment to becoming an increasingly important layer of financial services, with its role in investing extending beyond transaction automation to creating more contextual, responsive and easier-to-navigate investment experiences, said Ronit Kar, Director & CEO, ViewTrade International IFSC Private Limited (VTI IFSC). As India's investor base continues to expand, the challenge for the financial services industry is increasingly shifting from providing access to markets and information to helping investors navigate the growing volume and complexity of information available to them. According to SEBI, the number of unique individual demat holders increased from 2.82 crore in March 2019 to 8.96 crore by March 2024, with the regulator subsequently reporting 11.4 crore unique demat accounts. The expansion highlights the growing scale of India's investment ecosystem and the need for technology that can make investing more intuitive and contextual. “The opportunity for AI in investing is not simply about automating transactions or generating market insights. It is about making the investment experience more contextual, responsive and easier to navigate, while maintaining appropriate governance and investor safeguards. As access to markets expands, the industry must increasingly focus on helping investors make sense of the information surrounding their decisions, rather than simply giving them more information,” said Ronit Kar, Director & CEO, ViewTrade International IFSC Private Limited. Investors today have access to market prices, company disclosures, research reports, macroeconomic indicators, news and global developments almost instantaneously. However, access to information does not necessarily translate into better investment decisions. AI-enabled systems can potentially help organise and contextualise this information based on an investor's portfolio, investment horizon and requirements. Rather than simply delivering more alerts and data points, AI can help identify developments that may be more relevant to an investor and present them in a more accessible manner. This could also enable conversational interfaces through which investors can interact with financial information without having to navigate multiple dashboards, reports and data sources. The objective, however, is not to replace investor judgement or prescribe what investors should buy or sell. Instead, AI can support investors by making relevant information easier to understand and navigate. Personalisation in investing is often associated with product recommendations. However, AI could enable financial platforms to personalise the overall investment experience. Two investors may hold the same security but have different investment horizons, objectives, portfolio exposures and risk considerations. A standard market alert may therefore have different relevance for each investor. AI can help platforms interpret these differences and surface information accordingly, from prioritising portfolio-relevant developments to identifying changes that may require attention. The opportunity becomes particularly significant as investors gain greater access to international markets. Cross-border investing involves additional layers of complexity, including different market hours, currencies, regulatory environments, settlement processes, custody arrangements and information sources. Building a seamless global investing experience therefore requires more than a consumer-facing application. It requires infrastructure connecting market access, brokerage technology, execution, custody, market data and operational processes. AI can increasingly operate across these layers by helping institutions process information, automate workflows, identify anomalies and make fragmented sources of data more usable. For investors, much of this technology may remain invisible, and that could be precisely the point. The first major wave of financial technology focused heavily on automation, digitising processes such as account opening, transactions, reporting and portfolio monitoring. AI introduces another possibility: augmentation. For investment professionals, AI can potentially reduce the time required to analyse large volumes of research, monitor portfolios and identify relevant developments. For financial institutions, it can help streamline operational processes and connect fragmented workflows. For investors, it can make financial information more accessible and easier to understand. “AI should not necessarily replace human judgement in investing. Markets remain influenced by events that cannot always be predicted from historical patterns, while individual investment decisions depend on circumstances that algorithms may not fully capture. Its more productive role may be to improve the quality and speed of information available to human decision-makers,” Kar added. Infrastructure Will Define the Next Investment Experience As AI becomes more deeply embedded into investment platforms, the underlying technology infrastructure will become increasingly important. A seamless global investing journey may involve multiple systems working together across brokerage, execution, custody, market connectivity, data and compliance. API-driven infrastructure is making it possible for financial institutions, brokers, wealth platforms and fintechs to integrate these capabilities into their own experiences rather than building every component independently. This could shift the focus of investment technology from what investors can see on their screens to what the underlying infrastructure can enable. AI can function as an intelligence layer within this infrastructure, helping connect data, automate processes, support monitoring and create more responsive experiences without adding complexity for the end user. The increasing adoption of AI in financial services also brings greater responsibility. Investment decisions involve financial consequences, making data quality, cybersecurity, explainability, regulatory compliance and human oversight critical components of AI adoption. According to PwC's 2025 Global Asset & Wealth Management Report, global assets under management could grow from $139 trillion in 2024 to $200 trillion by 2030. The report also found that 69% of institutional investors are likely to allocate capital to asset managers developing stronger technology capabilities. These trends point towards a broader shift in which technology capabilities are increasingly becoming part of the investment proposition itself. The future of AI in investing may ultimately be defined by how effectively it can make complexity less visible to the investor. As financial institutions seek to provide increasingly sophisticated investment experiences without adding friction, the focus could shift towards platforms where complexity is managed by the underlying infrastructure while simplicity remains visible to the end user. This will require a combination of AI, high-quality data, robust market infrastructure, APIs, automation and strong governance. As access to global markets continues to expand, the next frontier of investment technology may therefore lie not simply in providing access to more markets or more information, but in helping investors navigate that expanding universe with greater clarity, relevance and trust.

results.title: Odisha Roadshows Attract Rs 18.65 Lakh Crore: Industries Minister
results.description: Bhubaneswar: An aggressive state-sponsored campaign to position Odisha as a premier industrial destination has drawn Rs 18.65 lakh crore in investment commitments across 365 companies over the past two years, backed by roughly Rs 105 crore in domestic and global outreach spending.
